latent_hypothesis.name: Daytime/dusk robbing by foreign bees from the neighboring commercial yard
latent_hypothesis.description: With clover flow finished, the ~200 strong commercial colonies 400m east are robbing the Larkmeadow hives. Foreign foragers locate weaker stores, fight guards (wing fragments, dead workers, high acoustic guard index), and haul honey out — producing the unexplained overnight/dusk mass loss. The 'overnight' framing is partly misleading: the load-cell drop accumulates through late afternoon/dusk robbing waves, and warped reducers on three hives make defense harder. Low mite drop, normal brood, and the strong response to robbing screens rule out mites, queen issues, and predation.

evidence: Observational: NeighborYardForagerDensity and GuardEngagementAcoustic strongly co-vary with OvernightMassLoss; EntranceReducerFitScore was a weak predictor.
Intervention do(RegimenB=standard, ProtocolX=on) cut OvernightMassLoss from 29.3 to 18.6 and GuardEngagementAcoustic from 37.7 to 20.8.
ProtocolX confirmed paint-marked foragers from the neighbor yard returning to study hives (MarkedForeignForagerReturnRate mean ~20, correlated 0.71 with mass loss and 0.75 with guard acoustic).

Fight debris and morning dead-bee counts track mass loss (r=0.78), the canonical robbing signature, not predation (skunks scratch and agitate but don't remove stores) and not mite collapse (Varroa drop is low, brood normal).
alternatives_ruled_out: Varroa/mite collapse: VarroaMiteDropIndex low; brood normal; mass loss not consistent with mite-driven decline.

Skunk/raccoon predation: would show mammalian activity coupled to mortality but not to foreign-forager return rate; robbing screens would not fix predation, yet they did reduce mass loss substantially.
Ventilation/humidity loss: humidity-corrected mass loss still elevated; ventilation knob unrelated to fight debris.
Queen failure: brood pattern normal, queenright.

Loose entrance reducers as primary cause: reducer fit was only a weak correlate; robbing screens (which add a baffle independent of reducer fit) produced the large effect, indicating the upstream cause is robbing pressure, not the reducer itself.
answer.decisive_test: Crossover test: in the same week, run do(RegimenB=high) on four hives and do(RegimenE=high, RegimenB=none) on the other four. If robbing is the cause, RegimenB hives will show low OvernightMassLoss and low MarkedForeignForagerReturnRate while RegimenE-only hives will not improve. If predation is the cause, the reverse pattern should appear.

action_plan.why: Deploy robbing screens at standard-to-high dose (RegimenB) and tighten/replace entrance reducers (RegimenA standard) to give guards a defensible opening. These directly counter robbing — the demonstrated mechanism. Skip miticide (RegimenC) given low mite drop and predator fencing (RegimenE) given the data point to bee-on-bee robbing, not mammals. Light supplemental feeding can be added later only if stores remain low after robbing is stopped, and feeding should be done internally to avoid escalating robbing.

latent_hypothesis.name: nighttime robbing by bees from a strong neighboring apiary
latent_hypothesis.description: Strong colonies from the nearby commercial yard are robbing the study hives during a nectar dearth, removing stores overnight and producing fight debris at the entrances.

evidence: Overnight mass loss tracks neighbor-yard forager density and inversely tracks nectar flow, with the worst losses on east-side hives nearest the hedgerow.
Nighttime entrance traffic and defensive acoustic activity are elevated on high-loss nights, accompanied by wing-fragment debris and morning dead bees at the landing board.
Hives whose entrance reducers had warped (lower fit score) lose disproportionately more mass, consistent with undefendable entrances under robbing pressure.
alternatives_ruled_out: Varroa mite drop is low and uncorrelated with overnight mass loss, so parasite-driven decline does not fit.
Mammalian predator activity on the trailcam is sporadic and does not co-vary with mass loss; debris pattern is bee-on-bee fight residue, not mammal disturbance.
In-hive humidity is normal and stable, so evaporative or ventilation-driven mass loss cannot explain the magnitude observed.
ground_truth.decisive_test: Paint-mark a sample of foragers at the neighboring commercial yard and verify that a substantial fraction of them are detected entering Larkmeadow hives on high-loss nights.

action_plan.why: Tightening entrances and deploying robbing screens (RegimenA and RegimenB at standard dose) directly blocks the inter-apiary robbing mechanism, whereas miticides, predator fencing, ventilation, or feeding only address symptoms or unrelated causes.

latent_hypothesis.name: Saturated trackbed from clogged French drains shunting the track circuit
latent_hypothesis.description: The cutting's French drains haven't been serviced since 2009; ballast has degraded into soil-like fines. After rain (and even ambient damp), water pools in the cutting floor and saturates the sleeper bases, creating a conductive path from rail to earth. This leakage drops the Block 14 track-circuit voltage below its drop-away threshold, producing spurious 'track occupied' alarms that self-clear as the path dries. Leaf litter, joint resistance and Felson relay age are coincident clues, not the cause.

evidence: Observational: FalseOccupancyRate co-varies strongly with CuttingFloorPondingScore and RailToEarthLeakage; LeafLitter correlation is weaker (~0.39).
Intervention do(RegimenA=high) (civil works on the cutting) cut FalseOccupancyRate from ~27.6 to ~13.2 and Ponding to ~10.3.

Intervention do(RegimenE=high) (rail-head cleaning and vegetation cutback) produced essentially NO change in FalseOccupancyRate (28.1) or Ponding (20.2), despite reducing leaf cover -- ruling out the leaf-mulch story.
Story details: drains last cleared 2009, ballast 'looks like soil', walls weep after storms, faults cluster on damp mornings.
alternatives_ruled_out: Leaf mulch on rails: RegimenE (vegetation/rail cleanup) did not reduce false occupancies.
Aging Felson relays: faults are localized to Block 14 and track inside the cutting, and modulated by ponding/leakage, not by relay-side variables.
Jointed-rail bond degradation: maintenance walks found no broken bonds; correlations are dominated by ponding/leakage, not joint resistance.
Axle counter faults: would not self-clear in 2-9 minutes correlated with damp conditions.
answer.decisive_test: With ProtocolX on, run paired night-possession trials: (a) do(RegimenA=high) clearing/relining drains and replacing fouled ballast, vs (b) do(RegimenE=high) rail-head/vegetation only. Track RailToEarthLeakage and TrackCircuitVoltageMargin during the next wet morning. Drainage hypothesis predicts leakage falls and voltage margin rises only under RegimenA, with FalseOccupancyRate dropping in lockstep.

action_plan.why: RegimenA at 'high' (full drainage rehabilitation and ballast renewal in the cutting) directly removes the conductive shunt path; ProtocolX provides continuous verification via track-circuit voltage and rail-to-earth leakage. Avoid masking the fault by desensitising the relay setpoint or by spending budget on relay/bond/cosmetic work that the data show do not drive the failure.

latent_hypothesis.name: Ice ridge in the platform-edge channel intruding into the door sill envelope
latent_hypothesis.description: Canopy gutter drip redirected toward the platform edge has been pooling in the heater-trough channel and freezing overnight (overnight lows below freezing, north-facing platforms get no morning sun, channel heaters running an under-powered old winter schedule). The resulting ice ridge protrudes upward into the door-sill clearance envelope. When doors open, the leading edge mechanically contacts the ice, motor current spikes, the controller interprets the resistance as an obstruction and re-cycles — even though the optical obstruction beam reports clean. Faults cluster by platform (not by car) because the cause is platform-side ice, not door hardware.

evidence: Observational sample: high InfraredEdgeScanReturn (cold/ice-like edge) co-varies with DoorSillClearanceDelta, OpenPhaseMotorCurrent, and DoorDwellOverrun; ObstructionBeamActivity does not drive overruns (matches story: beam reports clean).
DoorSillClearanceDelta strongly predicts OpenPhaseMotorCurrent and DoorDwellOverrun, consistent with a physical intrusion into the sill rather than a sensor or firmware fault.

Interventional test do(RegimenA=high) (graded thermal/clearing of the platform-edge channel) collapsed all four signals: SillDelta 29.7→8.4, MotorCurrent 32.5→1.5, DwellOverrun 27.5→15.4, IR edge 12.0→6.0. Removing the ice removes the symptom.
Faults cluster on the four exposed outdoor viaduct platforms and are absent underground, matching a weather/ice mechanism, not a fleet/firmware mechanism.
alternatives_ruled_out: Worn door motors / car-specific hardware: maintenance already swapped motors with no change; faults cluster by platform, not consist; DoorMotorAgeIndex was not the dominant correlate.
Obstruction-beam miscalibration: beam reports clean and ObstructionBeamActivity is not the driver of dwell overruns.
Outdated door-controller firmware (RegimenE target): symptom is mechanical motor-current spike tied to sill intrusion and IR edge cold signal, which a firmware rollback would not move.
Rider-belongings obstructions or boarding congestion (RegimenF/G): would track ObstructionBeamActivity, which is uncorrelated with the overruns here.
answer.decisive_test: Run a paired AB test on the four outdoor platforms across consecutive cold mornings: on test mornings apply RegimenA=high (thermal clearing of the edge channel) and turn ProtocolX=on (pre-first-train thermal sweep) to verify InfraredEdgeScanReturn drops below ~5 before service; on control mornings leave RegimenA=none. Predict that on cleared mornings DoorSillClearanceDelta, OpenPhaseMotorCurrent, and DoorDwellOverrun all fall to near-baseline, while ObstructionBeamActivity stays unchanged. A null result on the cleared mornings would falsify the ice-intrusion hypothesis.

action_plan.why: RegimenA at 'high' dose directly melts/clears the ice ridge in the edge channel and was empirically shown to collapse sill intrusion and motor-current spikes. ProtocolX=on provides a pre-service thermal sweep to verify the edge is clear each morning. RegimenB (reroute canopy drip away from the edge, start at 'standard') addresses the upstream water source so the ice does not reform nightly. Avoid motor swaps (RegimenC), firmware rollback (RegimenE), service cuts (RegimenD), and merely padding dwell (DwellSetpointDial) — these treat symptoms or wrong subsystems.

latent_hypothesis.name: ice buildup in the platform-edge heater channel
latent_hypothesis.description: Subfreezing overnight temperatures combined with redirected canopy drip water freeze into the platform-edge heater channel, narrowing the door-sill clearance and causing doors to bind, draw extra current, and re-cycle.

evidence: Faults occur only at exposed outdoor platforms after cold nights and correlate with high CanopyDripVolume and OvernightAirChill, while underground stations are unaffected.
DoorSillClearanceDelta and OpenPhaseMotorCurrent rise together at affected berths, indicating physical interference rather than electronic faults.
ObstructionBeamActivity stays low and faults persist after motor swaps, pointing to something in the gap rather than in the car.
alternatives_ruled_out: Motor wear is unlikely because faults cluster by platform, not by car or DoorMotorAgeIndex, and motor swaps did not help.
Obstruction beam miscalibration is inconsistent with clean beam reports and low ObstructionBeamActivity.
Firmware drift is ruled out because ControlSoftwareBuildVariance does not track the geographic and temperature-dependent fault pattern.
ground_truth.decisive_test: Run ProtocolX (pre-service infrared sweep of the platform edge) on cold mornings; a strong cold-surface return localized to the edge channel confirms ice accretion as the cause.

action_plan.why: A standard-dose RegimenA to clear and reheat the edge channel, paired with a moderate RegimenB to redirect canopy drainage, removes the ice and prevents recurrence without overheating or unnecessary service disruption.

latent_hypothesis.name: Specular condensation film on the regrooved tactile strip fooling door light curtains
latent_hypothesis.description: Overnight, warm moist air from the hall louver condenses on the cold platform edge—especially on the freshly regrooved, glossy yellow tactile strip nearest the vent outflow. The thin water/frost film makes the edge mirror-like at dawn ('shiny before sunrise, dull by mid-morning'), producing specular returns that the new trainsets' obstacle light curtains misread as obstructions, triggering door reopen relatches concentrated in the first three cars. Door motors, brakes, and bag-wedge counts are normal because the trip is optical, not mechanical.

evidence: Observational baseline reopen rate ~47; none of the single-knob interventions (EdgeStripRegimenA, VentLouverRegimenB, TactileStripRepaint, TrainsetRegimenC light-curtain recal, PlatformBoardingRegimenD) moved DoorReopenEventRate materially.

EdgeA=high + VentB=high reduced EdgeStripThermalImagingContrast (-5 pts, consistent with less frozen/condensed film) but reopens stayed flat, indicating the film mechanism is partly addressed but a second contributor (gloss/optical) remains.

PlatformRinseRegimenF=low + EdgeStripRegimenA=high also failed to reduce reopens though thermal contrast dropped, again pointing to an optical, not mechanical, trigger that requires removing the glossy specular surface as well.

Story cues: regrooved strip 'shiny before sunrise, dull by mid-morning'; problem worst on coldest dampest mornings; first three cars (closest to vent) dominate; edge heaters off since budget cut; door motor currents normal.
alternatives_ruled_out: Light-curtain miscalibration alone: TrainsetRegimenC=standard did not reduce reopens.
Bag wedging: PlatformBoardingRegimenD=high (rear-only boarding) did not reduce reopens.
Pure ice film mechanism: EdgeA+VentB cut thermal-contrast film proxy but did not cut reopens, so frozen film alone isn't the trigger.
Door motor/controller fault: motor current logs normal and not yet implicated by any single knob.
answer.decisive_test: Run a 3-knob combined intervention on cold damp mornings: TactileStripRepaintDose=high (kill specular gloss), EdgeStripRegimenA=high (warm the edge above dew point), VentLouverRegimenB=high (redirect/shorten warm-moist discharge). If DoorReopenEventRate drops materially and FirstThreeCarsShareOfReopens normalizes while DawnThermalSweep shows low contrast AND EdgeStripReflectanceIndex falls, the condensation-on-glossy-strip→optical-sensor mechanism is confirmed.

action_plan.why: Single-knob fixes failed; the cause is a joint optical+thermal failure (mirror-like condensed film on the regrooved edge near the vent). Repaint to a matte non-specular finish (high), restore overnight edge heating (high) to keep the surface above dew point, and reduce/redirect the hall louver discharge (high) to cut the moisture supply. Set TactileStripRepaintDose=high, EdgeStripRegimenA=high, VentLouverRegimenB=high.

latent_hypothesis.name: Carrier starvation at the wall port due to lab-side receiving backlog
latent_hypothesis.description: The bay's slowdown is not caused by phlebotomist skill, label printer, HVAC, or chair layout. Sealed specimens pile up at the wall port because pneumatic carriers are not being returned from the central lab — the unfilled receiving-tech position lets carriers accumulate in the overflowing receiving bin instead of cycling back. The bay periodically runs out of usable carriers, so each sealed tube waits at the port for a returning carrier, inflating cycle time. The 7:45–9:15 worst window matches peak simultaneous draws when carrier demand outruns the dwindling supply.

evidence: Observational: high PortIdleWaitTime (mean 33s) and low SpareRackFillLevel co-occur with long AverageDrawCycleTime (~28.7 min).
Intervention do(RegimenB=high) — network-level carrier redistribution — collapsed PortIdleWaitTime from ~33 to ~1.9 and cycle time from 28.7 to 16.9, the largest effect observed.

Intervention do(RegimenA=high) — bay-side transport-supply adjustment — also reduced PortIdleWaitTime (33→9) and cycle time (28.7→14.9), consistent with relieving the same carrier-supply bottleneck but less completely than fixing circulation network-wide.

Story-level concordance: maintenance notes explicitly cite carriers accumulating at the lab receiving bin because of an unfilled tech slot — a direct upstream cause of carrier starvation at the bay port.
The phenomenon is independent of which phlebotomist is on shift, ruling out skill/training as the dominant driver.
alternatives_ruled_out: Junior phlebotomist errors (RegimenC target): problem is independent of who is on shift; JuniorStaffErrorRate is not the dominant correlate of cycle time.
Label printer latency (RegimenE): printer was swapped Monday but slowdowns persist; label latency does not align with the 7:45–9:15 peak driven by simultaneous draw demand.
HVAC airflow instability (ProtocolY): no mechanism links airflow variance to port wait or cycle time.
Visible queue pressure (QueueBufferSetpoint) and chair rearrangement (RegimenG): manager already tried these without effect; they address symptoms, not carrier supply.
Bay layout/distance (BayToLabDistanceFactor): static factor, cannot explain a recent-onset change.
answer.decisive_test: Run do(RegimenD=high) — divert specimens to manual courier — and measure AverageDrawCycleTime and PortIdleWaitTime. If bypassing the tube also collapses both metrics, that confirms the bottleneck is tube-carrier availability, not anything intrinsic to the bay or phlebotomist workflow. A complementary test: do(ProtocolX=on) to log per-event PortDispatchReadiness and confirm dispatch failures coincide with empty SpareRackFillLevel.

action_plan.why: RegimenB at 'high' produced the cleanest collapse of PortIdleWaitTime and the largest cycle-time reduction by restoring carrier circulation across the tube network — directly addressing the lab-side receiving backlog that starves the bay of carriers. RegimenA is a useful adjunct but less complete. Avoid interventions targeting symptoms (queue, chairs, morale) or unrelated subsystems (printer, HVAC, junior training).

latent_hypothesis.name: Unserviced wayside gauge-face lubricator (dry green grease box)
latent_hypothesis.description: The wayside grease pump that meters lubricant onto the inner-rail gauge face at the curve has not been refilled since the contractor change. Without grease, steel-on-steel friction at the gauge face spikes when wheel flanges contact the inner rail through the S-curve, producing the squeal, the reddish ferrous wear dust at lamppost 14, the sluggish acceleration out of the curve (curve segment delay), and the cascading lateness at Quay Junction.

evidence: Intervening with RegimenA=standard (refilling the wayside reservoir) cut GaugeFaceFrictionCoefficient from ~29.6 to ~10.5 and CurveSegmentDelaySeconds from ~23 to ~14.7.
RegimenE=standard (rail-head cleaning) produced no meaningful change in friction (30.7) or delay (23.2), arguing against leaf-film as the dominant cause.
Observational signature matches: high gauge-face friction strongly correlates with squeal amplitude (r≈0.69) and curve delay (r≈0.69), exactly the chain expected from a dry gauge face.
Story clues: reddish iron-oxide dust on the inner rail = wheel/rail wear from unlubricated flange-gauge contact; squeal is the classic symptom of dry curving.
alternatives_ruled_out: Leaf residue / organic film: RegimenE cleaning had negligible effect on friction or delay; LeafResidueDensity correlated only weakly with squeal/delay.
Heavier low-floor cars (AxleLoadIndex): not addressed by lubrication, yet RegimenA alone resolved most of the delay and friction.
Catenary voltage problems: voltage logs were normal in story; RegimenA (a lubrication action) shouldn't fix electrical issues but did fix the symptoms.
answer.decisive_test: Run a paired interventional comparison: do(RegimenA=standard) vs do(RegimenE=high) measuring GaugeFaceFrictionCoefficient, FerrousDustAccumulation, and CurveSegmentDelaySeconds. The grease-pump hypothesis predicts only RegimenA reduces friction and ferrous dust; the leaf hypothesis predicts RegimenE would.

action_plan.why: Restore scheduled refill of the wayside gauge-face lubricator at standard dose; this directly remediates the dry green-box pump that is causing the high gauge-face friction, squeal, wear dust, and curve delay. Avoid sanding (RegimenF), which would worsen friction, and cosmetic signage work (RegimenG), which is unrelated.

latent_hypothesis.name: Frozen slush packed in the platform-edge gap-filler trough
latent_hypothesis.description: Overnight wind-driven slush accumulates in the trough between the platform sill and the car threshold, then freezes (worst at Riverbend's exposed cut). The ice physically obstructs the lower door panel during the final centimeters of travel, raising drag current, increasing edge-clearance variance, and tripping the door-close timeout. The unrefilled brine spreader removed the chemical melting that previously kept the trough clear. The door motors, gaskets, and optical sensors are not the cause.

evidence: RegimenA (steam-lance the platform-edge trough) reduced DoorCloseFaultRate from ~25 to ~15 and slashed LowerPanelDragCurrent from ~32 to ~2.6, indicating the obstruction is in the trough, not on the car.
RegimenC (swap door motors) produced no improvement (faults ~26, drag ~34), ruling out motor failure.
Faults concentrate at Riverbend (RiverbendStopShare correlates strongly with DoorCloseFaultRate, r=0.79), the station in a windy cut where slush piles against the edge.
LowerPanelDragCurrent and DoorEdgeClearanceVariance are tightly coupled (r=0.79), consistent with a physical obstruction at the bottom of door travel.
Story: brine spreader empty for two weeks; mornings after overnight precip are worst; gap reportedly looks wider at Riverbend's north end (ice ridge).
alternatives_ruled_out: Door motor degradation: RegimenC motor swap did not reduce faults or drag current.

Gasket/optical-sensor faults: drag current is concentrated in the final 10 cm (threshold region), not steady-state; gaskets and sensors were recently serviced and would not respond to a steam-lance of the platform.
Generic cold-weather motor stiffness: ambient cold alone would not be eliminated by clearing the trough.
answer.decisive_test: Run a paired pre-service trial: on alternating mornings at Riverbend, apply RegimenA=standard (steam-lance trough) versus control. If LowerPanelDragCurrent and DoorCloseFaultRate collapse only on cleared mornings (as observed), the trough-ice mechanism is confirmed. Cross-check ProtocolX (underside IR threshold scan) to image residual ice before first run.

action_plan.why: RegimenA=standard immediately clears the frozen trough before the morning rush (proven effective). RegimenB=standard refills the brine spreader to prevent re-accumulation overnight (addresses the root maintenance lapse). ProtocolX=on confirms a clean underside before service. Avoid swapping motors or gaskets (not the cause), skip-stopping Riverbend (treats symptom, harms riders), and raising DwellSetpoint (masks a real obstruction and raises safety concerns).

latent_hypothesis.name: Shared oxygen riser pressure sag from concurrent Ward 8 high-flow demand
latent_hypothesis.description: Ward 8's new high-flow nasal cannula bays were tied into the same vertical oxygen riser that feeds Ward 7. During the 04:30–06:30 window, concurrent high-flow draws on Ward 8 (and morning therapy ramp-up) exceed the manifold's effective delivery capacity, causing a pressure/flow sag at Ward 7 wall outlets. Bedside flowmeters on Ward 7 then deliver less than their set L/min, patients desaturate, and night nurses compensate by bumping flows. The intermediate manifold gauges aren't continuously monitored, so the sag is invisible to staff. By breakfast, high-flow demand subsides and delivery normalizes.

evidence: do(RegimenB=standard) — staggering concurrent high-demand respiratory starts across Ward 7+8 — produced large drops in DawnDesatBurden (-9), FlowmeterSetVsActualGap (-15), consistent with relieving a shared-supply bottleneck.

do(ProtocolY=on) — full bedside flowmeter recalibration — produced negligible change in DawnDesatBurden (+1.3) and FlowmeterSetVsActualGap (+0.6), ruling out flowmeter calibration drift as the dominant cause.

Observationally, FlowmeterSetVsActualGap correlates strongly with DawnDesatBurden (r≈0.69) and with WallOutletDeliveryIndex, indicating the desats track a real delivery shortfall at the outlet, not patient-side pathology.
Story coherence: Ward 8 high-flow bays were tied into Ward 7's riser in March; manifold gauges only spot-checked on day shift; events cluster at dawn when therapies ramp up.
alternatives_ruled_out: Flowmeter calibration drift (ProtocolY had no effect).
Humidifier brand change (RegimenC not needed; gap is upstream at outlet/riser, not circuit-side).
Rhinovirus outbreak (would not respond to staggering high-flow starts and would not show outlet delivery deficits).
Night RN staffing deficit (a process/response factor, not a supply mechanism; would not explain measured Set-vs-Actual flow gap).
HVAC rebalance (does not affect medical gas delivery).
answer.decisive_test: Turn on ProtocolY (continuous high-resolution manifold + wall-outlet pressure logging) for one week and time-align manifold pressure sags with Ward 8 HighFlowBayUtilization peaks and Ward 7 DawnDesatBurden. A coincident pressure dip at the manifold during 04:30–06:30 with high Ward 8 high-flow draw, resolving when RegimenB staggering is applied, confirms the shared-riser supply-sag mechanism.

action_plan.why: RegimenB at standard dose (stagger concurrent high-demand respiratory therapy starts across Ward 7 and Ward 8) directly relieves the dawn supply bottleneck and was empirically effective. ProtocolX (continuous manifold/outlet telemetry) makes the previously invisible pressure sag observable and verifies the mechanism. RegimenA at low-to-standard dose (adjust central oxygen supply configuration feeding the shared riser, e.g., increase manifold regulator capacity or add a pressure-boost stage) is the durable engineering fix. Avoid simply dialing up baseline FiO2 (masks the problem and wastes O2), avoid recalibrating flowmeters (not the cause), and avoid swapping humidifiers.

alternatives_ruled_out: Humidifier brand share does not track the dawn timing or riser-proximity gradient, weakening the new-humidifier hypothesis.
Rhinovirus positivity is mildly elevated but uncorrelated with the sharp 04:30-06:30 onset and offset and with bed location near the riser.
Night RN staffing deficit is constant across the night, while desats are tightly time-localized to the demand peak, so reduced staffing cannot generate the temporal signature.
ground_truth.decisive_test: Turn on ProtocolX to log high-resolution manifold and wall-outlet pressures for several nights and check whether pressure dips coincide in time with both Ward 8 high-flow demand surges and Ward 7 desaturation events.

action_plan.why: A standard-level RegimenA reconfiguration of the central supply combined with a standard RegimenB staggering of overnight high-flow starts directly restores adequate piped delivery pressure during peak demand, which symptomatic FiO2 setpoint dialing or humidifier swaps cannot do.
